TOKEN2049: Fundamentals Are Shaping Crypto Investing
Bernd Schmid, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 2:05 PM MST 10 min read

Two days at the biggest crypto conference in the world are exciting. It's also exhausting listening to and meeting with so many of the major builders and thought leaders from both the crypto and the traditional finance world. I took it in for you, and this article is to share some of my major takeaways -- many of which you're less likely to read anywhere else -- but that I think are very encouraging for Foolish crypto investors.

Let me present to you the story of why right now is exactly the right time for Foolish investors to enter the digital asset space. It comes in five chapters, plus a bonus for the truly Foolish investors.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Past Hype Has Led to the Availability of Highly Usable Infrastructure Today

Alliance's Will Robinson shared a few charts based on hundreds, if not thousands, of conversations with crypto founders. They depict what founders have in mind for building applications over time.

Nonfungible tokens (NFTs), for example, had the highest share in November 2021, with 37% of all founders. This dropped quickly and kept dropping to basically zero right now. The decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) had a peak later in December 2021 at 24%, dropping to less than 4% a year later and are at almost zero now. Other themes, such as play-to-earn, show virtually the same curves. One theme that may have just peaked and is already dropping sharply is prediction markets.

This is not surprising. New things cause hypes that then quickly subside. This may never change because it's human nature. We have to consider such cycles in our fundamental investing approach, being careful about when and how we buy into hype.

But something has changed in crypto that makes it easier for fundamental investors to succeed. Real Vision's Jamie Coutts pointed this out very well in his presentation.

The above-mentioned hypes led to massive investments into building and scaling infrastructure. In 2021, for example, $36.5 billion was raised, according to Coutts. This paid off in a sense because we now have massive blockspace available across diverse ecosystems, and it costs very little to use. Even the notoriously slow and expensive Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) blockchain went from a median fee of more than $10 in 2021 to just around $0.04 now.

title: Dell vs. Nvidia: Chip Stocks Just Suffered Their Worst Sell-Off Since 2020. Which Is the Better Buy for 2027?
detail:
Dell vs. Nvidia: Chip Stocks Just Suffered Their Worst Sell-Off Since 2020. Which Is the Better Buy for 2027?
RJ Fulton, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 12:50 PM MST 5 min read
DELL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has fueled extraordinary growth across the technology sector, but a recent sell-off has Wall Street questioning whether massive infrastructure investments can continue to justify elevated valuations. For investors looking toward 2027, the pullback presents an opportunity to reassess two major beneficiaries of the AI boom: Dell Technologies(NYSE:DELL) and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA).

Dell provides the servers and infrastructure needed to support AI workloads, while Nvidia designs the advanced chips powering them. Both have benefited from surging demand, but their business models, profitability, and valuations differ substantially. As investors become more selective about AI exposure, those differences could determine which stock offers the more compelling long-term opportunity.

The case for Dell Technologies

Dell provides servers, storage systems, and personal computers to enterprises, governments, and cloud providers. Its Infrastructure Solutions Group has become an increasingly important driver of growth as demand for AI-optimized servers accelerates.

In fiscal 2026, Dell generated $113.5 billion in revenue, an increase of approximately 19% year over year. Net income reached $5.9 billion, representing a profit margin of 5.2%. More recent results highlight the momentum behind its AI business. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenue surged 58% to $47 billion, with AI-optimized server revenue doubling to $16.4 billion. Dell also reported a $95 billion AI server backlog, providing considerable visibility into future demand, although orders remain subject to customer spending decisions.

At the end of fiscal 2026, its debt-to-equity ratio was negative due to a shareholder equity deficit, while its current ratio stood near 0.9x. Nevertheless, the company generated substantial operating cash flow, providing resources to fund operations and return capital to shareholders.

The case for NVIDIA

NVIDIA is a leader in semiconductor stocks, supplying the GPUs, networking equipment, and software infrastructure powering much of the industry's expansion.

In fiscal 2026, Nvidia generated $215.9 billion in revenue, an increase of approximately 65% year over year. Net income reached $120.1 billion, representing an exceptional profit margin of 55.6%. More recent results highlight continued momentum. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenue surged 106% to $96.2 billion, driven by a 117% increase in data center revenue to $89 billion.

Nvidia also maintains an exceptionally strong financial position. At the end of fiscal 2026, its debt-to-equity ratio stood near 0.1x, while its current ratio was approximately 3.9x. The company generated roughly $96.6 billion in free cash flow during the year, providing substantial financial flexibility to invest in new technologies.

title: American Express Has Cut Its Share Count by 27% Since 2016. Here's What That Did for the Stock.

American Express Has Cut Its Share Count by 27% Since 2016. Here's What That Did for the Stock.
Neil Patel, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 1:50 PM MST 4 min read
AXP
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Companies that generate positive operating cash flow can allocate their capital in various ways. Of course, reinvesting in the business is what many long-term investors appreciate, as it can boost intrinsic value over time. There are also mergers and acquisitions, as well as paying down debt.

When it comes to returning capital to investors, companies can direct cash to dividend payments. Stock buybacks are another avenue to put money back into shareholders' pockets, particularly in a more tax-efficient manner.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

American Express (NYSE: AXP) has been a leader in the latter category. The premium credit card enterprise reduced its outstanding share count by a notable 26.8% from Q3 2016 to Q3 2026 (ended Sept. 30). Here's what this did for the financial stock.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Share buybacks lifted per-share earnings

Over the past decade, American Express has been a wildly successful investment asset. The stock produced a total return of 471% during that time (as of Nov. 4). This gain easily outpaced the S&P 500 index.

Profit growth is a critical catalyst that supports stock performance. From the third quarter of 2016 to the most recent quarter, American Express's diluted earnings per share (EPS) increased by 352%. This reveals major fundamental strength for the business.

The company's diluted EPS rose at a faster clip than net income, which was up 228% in the last 10 years. Share repurchases make up the difference. Every time the business chooses to conduct stock buybacks, it boosts the per-share profits attributable to each existing investor. In other words, shareholders see their ownership stakes steadily increase over time. This is a key part of the management team's capital allocation policy.

A high-quality compounder at a reasonable price

Investors shouldn't only buy a stock because the business is constantly repurchasing shares. There is always more to the thesis. That being said, American Express is a high-quality company that's worth looking into.

The business has established a strong position in the credit card market, with a wide economic moat supported by its robust brand, which attracts affluent customers, and its powerful network effect, which creates a positive feedback loop that improves the value proposition for consumers and merchants. These traits defend American Express's competitive standing.

title: IREN CEO: Old Nvidia H100s Just Recontracted at “Double the Original Contract Price”

IREN CEO: Old Nvidia H100s Just Recontracted at “Double the Original Contract Price”

IREN CEO: Old Nvidia H100s Just Recontracted at "Double the Original Contract Price" ©@Handmadefont from Handmadefont via Canva
Key Takeaways

IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts said on the company's Nov. 5 earnings call that older NVIDIA H100 GPUs were just recontracted at double their original contract price.

Old chips earning more on a second contract supports IREN's revenue and the useful life of NVIDIA's installed base.

IREN's capital spending reached $4.82 billion in the September 2026 quarter, and short seller Jim Chanos argues its capital base is too big for its revenue.

A new contract with a customer prepaying about 90% of the GPU capex answers part of that worry, and IREN traded at 3.1x forward sales on Nov. 2, below its three-year average of 5.2x.

IREN (IREN:NASDAQ) went into its Nov. 5 report after a roughly 20% slide, on news from The Information that delays at its Childress, Texas site held up some of Microsoft's AI spending.

Then co-founder and co-CEO Daniel Roberts gave NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) shareholders a line worth hearing on IREN's fiscal first-quarter call:

"Older generation H100s, we just recontracted at double the original contract price."

Which is a remarkable thing to say about hardware that old.

And IREN isn't the only one seeing it. As Dave Blundin put it on this week's episode of Moonshots with Peter Diamandis: "we're seeing H100 prices increasing, which is insane, on chips that are how old? Three years old now."

Old chips that still earn

The worry about GPU clouds has been that the chips lose their value before they pay off. IREN's own math on its Microsoft contract assumed its GPUs would be worth nothing after five years.

If a three-year-old H100 can rent for twice its first contract, that assumption looks conservative. That's good news for IREN, which keeps each GPU when a contract ends. It's good news for NVIDIA too, since its chips are still earning money for its customers years after they shipped.

IREN's newest deals point the same way. In the days before the call, it signed a five-year contract at about $22 million of annualized revenue per megawatt and a shorter one at more than $40 million, Roberts said. A leading frontier AI lab also expanded its capacity with IREN again.

Analysts already expected IREN's revenue to roughly quadruple, from $707 million in fiscal 2026 to $2.81 billion in fiscal 2027 (the year ending June 2027), then reach $7.41 billion the year after.

NVIDIA (NVDA) plunged 9% in one day, erasing about $450 billion in market value and dropping Jensen Huang from ninth to 13th richest.

Fears that costlier borrowing and delayed data center construction could slow AI spending drove the selloff, yet NVIDIA's reported results show no slowdown.

Jensen Huang lost $15.1 billion on paper on November 5, 2026, and the drop pushed him from ninth to 13th on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. It was his biggest one-day dollar loss since January 27, 2025, and it left his fortune at $150.9 billion.

pestoverde / Flickr

The loss came from his company's stock. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) fell $18.53, or 9.26%, to close at $181.60, its biggest one-day drop since January 2025. About $450 billion of market value disappeared, leaving the company worth $4.39 trillion.

NVDA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

The selloff followed the Democratic sweep of the November 3 midterm elections. Investors pointed to fears that costlier borrowing and possible delays in data center construction could slow AI spending. Nothing in NVIDIA's reported results shows that slowdown yet. Shareholders will test that gap between fear and reported results in the coming weeks.

Why Huang's Ranking Moves With NVIDIA Shares

Most of Huang's fortune is his roughly 3.4% NVIDIA stake, held in his own name and in family trusts according to a September 2026 filing. His ranking is effectively a live gauge of NVIDIA's market value, which is why his 9.1% wealth decline tracked the stock's fall.

The three Walton siblings now sit directly above him, led by Jim Walton in 10th at $155 billion, about $4 billion ahead. A competing real-time list still had Huang ninth late on November 5. The 500 richest people lost a combined $185 billion, the 14th-largest one-day drop since the index began in 2012.

title: Sandisk Stock Has Lost About 64% Since June. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy It.
detail:
Sandisk Stock Has Lost About 64% Since June. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy It.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 2:07 PM MST 5 min read
SNDK
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) stock sank about 22% on Thursday, Nov. 5, adding to a painful stretch for the flash memory maker. At roughly $806 as of this writing, shares are down about 64% from their June 25 close of $2,335, a record.

Thursday's slide continued a sell-off in AI data center stocks that started after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, as investors weighed whether the outcome might slow data center construction.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

And it's been quick. Sandisk closed around $1,330 on Oct. 29, the day it posted fiscal first-quarter results and guided for even higher profits in this quarter. So the growth stock has fallen about 39% over the past week, even though the company's outlook calls for earnings to keep rising.

I think the sell-off has finally brought the stock to a price worth paying. And Sandisk's guidance is what I'd use to set it.

Image source: Getty Images.

Earnings are still rising, just more slowly

Showing how much the company has changed, Sandisk's earnings per share on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis grew 26% sequentially, to $49.51 in its fiscal first quarter of 2027 (which ended Oct. 2, 2026). That followed sequential gains of 278% in fiscal Q3 of 2026 and 68% in fiscal Q4. Fiscal Q1 revenue came to $11.0 billion, up 23% sequentially and 378% year over year, and data center customers accounted for about $4.8 billion of it. For fiscal Q2, management guided to adjusted earnings of $55 to $57 per share, implying about 13% growth over fiscal Q1 at the midpoint.

Put simply, profits are still climbing. But the growth rate is slowing quickly, and it might keep falling from here.

After all, memory profits can swing fast. A year before, in fiscal Q1 of 2026, Sandisk earned just $1.22 per share on an adjusted basis, with a gross margin of around 30%.

And in the three months ended March 28, 2025, it had an adjusted loss of $0.30 a share.

True, the company looks different now. Data center revenue was under $300 million in the year-ago quarter, and the gross margin has since climbed to 85%. But flash memory is still a product whose price can fall when supply outruns demand, and Sandisk's earnings would probably drop with it.

The stock is priced for a brief boom

Sandisk's guidance covers only one quarter, so the simplest way to use it is to annualize it. Four quarters at the $56 midpoint would total about $224 per share in adjusted profit. At around $806, the stock trades at under 4 times those annualized earnings.
